module_title: The Operative Portion, Sentencing Hearing, and Victim Compensation
introduction: Tailored for Judicial Service Mains, this level explores the climax of a criminal trial. It details the mandatory separate hearing for deciding punishment, the calculation of concurrent vs. consecutive sentences, and the shift toward victim-centric justice in the 2023 reforms.

core_concepts.title: The Sentencing Hearing (Section 258(2), BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
In India, conviction and sentencing are a two-step process in warrant trials.
- The Rule: If a judge convicts the accused, they MUST pause the trial and hear the accused on the question of sentence before actually passing the sentence.
- Purpose: To allow the accused to present mitigating circumstances (e.g., young age, first-time offender, sole breadwinner) to secure a lesser punishment. Failure to hold this separate hearing is a fatal procedural flaw.

core_concepts.title: The Operative Paragraph (Conviction & Sentence)
core_concepts.description:
The exact wording of the final order.
- Structure: The judge must explicitly state: 'The accused is hereby convicted under Section [X] of the BNS.' Followed by the sentence: 'He is sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) for [X] years and to pay a fine of ₹[Y], in default of which he shall undergo simple imprisonment for [Z] months.'
- Set-off (Section 475 BNSS): The judge MUST state that the period already spent by the accused in jail during the investigation/trial shall be set off against the final sentence.

core_concepts.title: Concurrent vs. Consecutive Sentences (Section 31, BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
If a person is convicted of 3 separate offenses (e.g., getting 3 years, 2 years, and 1 year).
- Consecutive (Default): The sentences run one after the other (Total = 6 years in jail).
- Concurrent: The judge can explicitly direct the sentences to run concurrently (simultaneously). The accused will only serve the longest individual sentence (Total = 3 years). Most judges order concurrent sentences unless the crime is exceptionally heinous.

core_concepts.title: Victim Compensation (Section 395, BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
A major focus of the new BNSS 2023.
- The Rule: When imposing a fine, the Court may order the whole or any part of the fine to be paid as compensation to the victim for any loss or injury caused by the offense.
- Furthermore, Section 396 BNSS creates a mandatory 'Victim Compensation Scheme' funded by the State to compensate victims of acid attacks, rape, and severe crimes, even if the offender is not traced or identified.

important_entities.name: Probation of Offenders Act, 1958
important_entities.significance: A judge must apply their mind to this Act before sending a convict to jail. For minor offenses, instead of sending the person to prison, the judge can release them after an admonition (warning) or on a bond of good conduct, to prevent first-time offenders from turning into hardened criminals in jail.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a Sessions Judge awards the Death Penalty, can the execution happen immediately? **NO**. Under Section 407 BNSS, a death sentence passed by a Court of Session MUST be submitted to the High Court for confirmation. It cannot be executed unless the High Court officially confirms it.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: C I F D S (Conviction section, Imprisonment term, Fine amount, Default jail term, Set-off)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Before finishing your draft judgment, ensure your final paragraph hits all 5 CIFDS markers to secure maximum marks.

exam_strategy_tips: In a Judiciary Mains Criminal Judgment paper, always write a dedicated subheading titled 'HEARING ON QUANTUM OF SENTENCE' after recording the conviction, to show the examiner you know the mandatory two-step procedure.
